analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 39, Alphonse Wartus versus the people of the state of Illinois. Mr. Fisher, Mr. Justice, would you please the court? This is a criminal case. I represent a prisoner in the Illinois penitentiary. He's serving a sentence, a life sentence, for bank robbery. This court granted his petition for certiorari from the Illinois Supreme Court's affirmance of his conviction and appointed counsel for petition. Our principal contention is that the state of Illinois has not accorded petitioner due process of law under the 14th Amendment. We submit that the facts of this case show a disregard of due process in several quite different respects. The variety of bad procedures that were applied to this man is striking. The procedural facts surrounding his trial are malodorous. But the court need not reach the doctrine of the facts as a whole being so shocking as to deny due process. We contend that they are, but the specific denials of due process are in themselves quite sufficient grounds for reversing. The two most critical issues are, first, that Illinois tried him over again after he had been acquitted by a federal court. And second, and it is an entirely separate and independent ground of reversal, that Illinois convicted him on the basis of unconstitutional activities of federal officers. Here are the facts, and they are not disputed. In 1953, a savings and loan association in Cook County was robbed by two armed men. They took some $4,000 and fled in a car. The driver was waiting in the car. The petitioner, then 26 years old, heard that he was wanted and he went to the United States Marshal's office where he was arrested and charged with being the driver of that car. And his defense was simply that they had the wrong man. At the trial petitioner, the identity of the driver of the car was the only issue. He took the stand. He and other witnesses testified that he was far away from the robbery at the time it occurred, and the testimony against him was by alleged accomplices. This trial was in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, and it was for violation of the Federal Bank Robbery Act. The basis of federal jurisdiction was the Savings and Loan Association, which was robbed, was federally insured by the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation. Incidentally, 94 percent of all savings and loan associations in this country are federally insured. And the existence of the insurance was stipulated in this case. Do you have the percentages on banks also, Mr. Fisher? That are insured by the FDIC? I think 87 percent of banks, as I recall, are insured. That's of both state and national banks. Yes. Thank you. As all banks, national and state are 14,777 only, are not insured by the FDIC. The petitioner was found not guilty by the Federal jury and was acquitted. Now we come to the facts bearing on our other point, the activities of the Federal officers. The United States District Judge was dissatisfied with the verdict, and he proceeded to criticize the jury in most unusual fashion. Some of the details are in our brief. The judge's conduct and the widespread publicity that was given to it were of a nature to encourage the retrial of the petitioner in the state court. And the state's attorney of Cook County said on the record that the Federal authorities came to him after petitioner's Federal acquittal. The petitioner was turned over to state custody and indicted a second time for this same robbery. Was your man the only defendant in the criminal in the Federal case? In the Federal case, he had two accomplices. But they were not tried with him. They were not tried with him. He was the sole defendant. He was the sole defendant. Did they plead guilty with it? Did they plead guilty? They weren't tried. Were they indicted? I don't think they were indicted at this time. I'm not sure of that. I don't think the record shows. They were, I happen to know, I don't think Mr. Wines would object, they were subsequently, placed under, under the Federal, under parole, under the Federal Parole Act. Now, in spite of a federal, of petitioner's acquittal by the Federal Court, the Federal Government kept on working for his conviction. The FBI agents, in disregard, as we contend, of the double jeopardy provision of the Fifth Amendment, interviewed one of petitioner's alibi witnesses and turned over the information to the state authorities. A special agent and a United States attorney also interviewed an entirely new witness, one who had not testified in the previous case, and they asked the new witness to come into the state court and testify. The Federal agents did the interviewing. The Illinois prosecutor did not talk with this new witness until the day he testified at the state trial. This activity of the Federal officers, as I say, is an entirely independent ground of reversal, separate from the former acquittal point. Mr. Fisher, are all these facts that you've recited thus far, I suppose the full record is the record in the Federal trial before us? Mr. Fisher, that was not, that was not put in issue in this case. But the case was tried on the basis that the issues were the same except for the alibi. The Supreme Court of Illinois so treated the matter. Mr. Fisher, I didn't mean, I didn't mean the substantive prosecutions, but the recitals that you gave, the conduct of the district judge and the activities of the Federal officials. Are they in the record? Mr. Fisher, they're all in there. Mr. Fisher, they're in either the brief or that book. Mr. Fisher, either our brief or in that record. Mr. Fisher, a stenographic record, isn't it? The clerk. The stenographic records with the clerk. Except the fact that I mentioned about what happened to the accomplices, alleged accomplices, subsequently that, that I did. Mr. Fisher, can we look at the proceedings, should it be deemed relevant in the district court, the United States District Court? Mr. Fisher, he was acquitted so that no certificate of evidence was made and there is a, there is a, a, a, a, a, a, a, record of it. Mr. Fisher, that's what I mean. Mr. Fisher, that's not in evidence in any way. Mr. Fisher, for instance, the remarks you, you... Mr. Fisher, it's not certified or in evidence. Mr. Fisher, you found some relevance to the remarks of the judge and etc. Mr. Fisher, those, those remarks are from newspaper clippings in the Chicago Press that I've Appended to my brief and I felt justified in doing that because this became such a famous matter that this judge attempted to defend himself in another case and his action in this case if they were so severely criticized in Chicago that he attempted to defend himself and it came into the record another case went up to the Court of Appeals for our circuit and there was discussed by both the majority and the dissenting judge as a matter of common knowledge, and it appears to be done under those circumstances that this court could take judicial notice of those facts. It's because I assume it may be relevant that I'm asking whether the materials are here before us. Yes. All right. It's our position is that the federal officers utilize the state court as their instrument in doing what the federal government is forbidden to do by the double jeopardy provision of the Fifth Amendment. And that we submit is not through process of law under the Fourteenth Amendment. The issue, as I've said, in the second trial is the same as that in the first trial. Well, I'm sorry to interrupt you again, but if you have your last statement, it becomes very important. If your contention is that the activities of federal officials from the Judge Downs constituted a violation of the double jeopardy of the Fifth Amendment as an injunction upon federal activities, then it becomes very important that all the materials bearing on that be properly before this court. Those materials were in the record as to the activities of these officers. To test the fact that the interviewing of the witnesses and turning over the evidence to the state authorities is in the record, Mr. Justice. The only thing that I said was not in the record and from the newspaper clippings were the statements of the federal district judge. The issue in the second trial, as I've said, is the same as in the first, and that issue was the identity of the person driving the car, using the escape. This is all perfectly clear from the opinion of the Illinois Supreme Court and is not disputed. And petitioner was found guilty in the second case. Now, the reason why he received life imprisonment was because it was mandatory under the Illinois Second Offender Statute, then in force. That statute provided that a prior conviction in a different case be mentioned in the indictment and brought to the attention of the juror. And there are statutes like that in a number of states. And that feature of the statute, however, I am glad to say, has been repealed this year so that Illinois is no longer in what I regard as the disgraceful position where juries are told of former offenses, where they must be told of former offenses if the habitual criminal feature is to be used. If the Second Offender feature is to be used, you have to put it in the indictment under this old statute. But, of course, the repeal is not retroactive and does not apply to my client. Now, in addition to these two points I have mentioned, and we do in our brief raise as an independent ground of reversal what we regard as an extremely unfair application of that provision to this case. And I'm sure we will not have time today to argue it orally. Today I want to argue three grounds of reversal orally, and they're separate and independent grounds of each other. One is the petitioner was tried over again after being acquitted for identically the same affair. The second is the unconstitutional participation of the federal officers. And the third is encroachment of the state of Illinois on the judicial power of the United States. Now, on our first point, it's undisputed that the second trial differed from the first in only two respects. The fact that the federal insurance did not have to be proved in the state case. And the second trial occurred in the state court rather than the federal court. Those are the only differences. Now, such differences have been thought in various cases to permit double prosecutions. But we disagree, and we contend that from the standpoint of due process, those two differences are not of a nature to justify a second trial for what is, in fact, the same offense. Due process is, of course, a matter of substance. And this question is an open question for this court, as I propose to show. Putting it in other words, I propose to show that it was the same offense in both trials, the same offense in both trials, and that the matter of the difference in jurisdictions ought not to make any difference. Now, of course, our premise is that under the 14th Amendment, the state of Illinois, by itself, may not keep on prosecuting a man after he has been acquitted. Our position here is based on the defense, in this big part of our case, our position is based on the defense of former acquittal, not on double jeopardy as a whole. We contend that the inviolability of a former acquittal is part of due process of law. And Palco against Connecticut and other cases of this court have expressly left that question open. In our brief... You mean that if he had been convicted in the federal trial, that you think you say he could have been retried again? I don't think... In Illinois? I don't think he ought to be, I'm candid to say, Mr. Justice, that that is not our case. Our case is acquittal, and acquittal is thoroughly distinguishable from former conviction. It has been distinguished, as we show in our briefs, since the time of the yearbooks. It's an absolutely fundamental part of ordered liberty. It goes back way behind the floor of the right of counsel, and it is, if you think the defense of former conviction, which is always a separate plea of common law, if you feel that that is a separate matter and is important and is part of the due process, why former acquittal is even more sacred. Now today, I'm going to assume that it is clear beyond doubt that Illinois couldn't try a man who'd been acquitted over again for identically the same thing. I mean, take the example, which is not our case, that they try for something that is admittedly the same offense under identically the same statute. I don't believe that Illinois would seriously contend that it would keep on trying a man over again under the same statute for the same offense constitutional. I'd say we have lots of material, but I will assume it now. Now, leaving aside for the moment the matter of the two jurisdictions, the state and the federal, we contend that the federal and state offenses are the same offense for purposes of double jeopardy. In other words, before we get to the matter of the two jurisdictions, I must first persuade you that neither the federal government acting alone nor the state acting alone could try a man twice for the same act of robbery under two federal statutes that are as similar as these two statutes here or under two state statutes that differ no more than the two statutes in this case. That's what I must persuade you first. Later, we reach our position that what they cannot do separately, they cannot do in combination. Defendant was tried the second time for identically the same conduct as in the first trial. He wasn't accused of robbing different banks or different people as in the whole case that has been set to follow this case in argument. Our case now is not a case involving fragmentation of crime for purposes of increasing the punishment. That's like the Ladner case which comes after the Hogue case that has been set in this group of three. Ladner is a punishment case. It's not a double jeopardy case at all. There was only one trial. You can't have double jeopardy unless there are two trials. And what is an appropriate unit of crime, unit of the crime, or unit of prosecution is a different thing in punishment cases than it is in a double jeopardy case that the appropriate unit might permit a man's punishment to be increased if he cuts more mailbags, for example, or if he steals more money. But that doesn't mean that a man can constitutionally be retried for each unit or for each piece of paper money. Punishment can be graded for the size and number of the offense. It's clear from reading all these cases that there is no such thing as a unit of the crime for all purposes. Now this court has ruled that there are two offenses for purposes of double jeopardy and each statute requires proof of an additional fact which the other statute does not. But surely this is basic. That separate fact must have some significance. Some significance in the way of a separate statutory purpose or policy. And I think I can demonstrate that. The Federal Bank Robbery Act makes it a crime to rob a national bank, a member of the Federal Reserve System, a member of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. And maybe those are separate offenses now. But let's suppose that Congress removes all questions and specifically makes them separate offenses. In similar fashion, Illinois could, of course, make separate offenses of robbing a state bank, a member of the Federal Reserve System, a member of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the states, of course, are free to protect federal institutions, a separate offense of robbery in a bank building, robbery after nightfall, robbery with a gun, robbery with a mask, a dozen more offenses, each with its unique fact to be proved as required by that statute. And those would be perfectly good separate offenses for purposes of counts and for purposes of punishment, for purposes of the prosecutor's option as to which he shall try. But it is a very different thing to say that they create separate offenses so as to allow a man to be acquitted one or more times and then tried over and over again for the same transaction. I'm sure this court would never stand for it. Unless this separate fact in each of these statutes reflects some separate purpose or policy, to permit retrials would reduce the Constitution, would deprive the Constitution of substance. From what do you derive the difference in your qualification, interestingly, unless it represents some different purpose? of policy. From what do you derive the difference in purpose of policy? It's the function of this court, it seems to me, to decide whether a difference is a difference of words merely, a verbal difference, a difference of trivialities, or a difference of constitutional substance. And to say that you could, that a man can be tried twice federally, I'm not talking about the two jurisdictions now, twice federally or twice by a state for robbing the same institution because one time it's a member of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and another time because it's a member of the Federal Reserve System, is something I'm certain this court would never stand for as a matter of constitutional law. That's not what the Constitution is. I suppose knocking down a postman in the post office building in Chicago, which is both an obstruction of the males if he's carrying a mailbag, and also an assault on the assimilation statute, you would say that those are two clearly different purposes. Is that it? No, no. You wouldn't? Not unless the males are being interfered with. Well, I'm saying he's trying to deliver something, and he's... That might easily be a separate purpose. It's up to this court. This court must decide each time whether there is substance in the difference or not. You must decide whether it's a matter of form or a matter of substance. You can take the case of a man being convicted of assault in the state, and then being tried federally for deprivation of the civil right to vote. It would appear there very strong ground to argue. It would seem to me there was a separate policy there, quite a separate policy. But this bank robbery statute is not that kind of a statute. The legislative history of the Bank Robbery Act makes it clear that the only purpose of the Bank Robbery Act was to assist state enforcement, to provide the resources of federal enforcement, to help stop roaming gang or state gangs of bank robbers. It might make a difference if the punishments are drastically different, and the amount of crude bank robbery involving elements of violence and interference with some other aspects of banking might merely be something with a small punishment that interferes with something else. I'm not thinking it is. Yes, of course, it would be a different policy. The standard case in the textbooks is that of a man who's tried for selling liquor to a miner on Sunday. There are two entirely different statutory purposes there. And you might have given the case in my case, for example. My man was accused of being in the getaway car. Now suppose he'd been tried for illegal parking by a hybrid. That would be an entirely separate purpose. And this was brought out in the case that is cited in this court, the case of this court that is often cited in this connection. That's the Gaviar case from the Philippine Islands. And that case is cited over and over again for the state that has repeated its two statutes, its two offenses, if there are two separate statutory requirements. But in the Gaviar case itself, in the opinion of that court, the court referred to the separate gist of the two statutes there involved. They were rather minor offenses, but to mind the court in Gaviar, the man was tried one time for creating a brawl under Philippine law, another time for insulting an official. And the court found, the court went into the inquiry and inquired as to the gist of the offenses. They referred to it right there. And they said these offenses have a different gist. Sometimes the word gravamen is used. Social purpose or policy is sometimes used. But there is no difference in these bank robbery statutes. The federal act, as I say, was simply concerned with enforcement. And the jurisdictional requirement, the jurisdictional requirement of federal insurance in the case of bank robbery is like the jurisdictional requirement that for Illinois to prosecute, the offense must be committed in Illinois. That must be proved. Mr. Wyand, the first of that, I believe, in one of the earlier briefs in the case. That's not his. Of course, the act was committed in Illinois. Well, here, we had to prove the jurisdictional requirement. The jurisdictional requirement had to be proved that this institution, this robbed institution, was insured. A decision for petitioner would not create a precedent against retrials in civil rights cases or in any other case where the court inquires into the matter to find out whether there's a substantial difference in these statutes. In our reply brief on page five, we show how foreign countries will not retry a man who's been acquitted in another country. The notion that because there are two sovereigns that you should try a man over again is not only unfounded in as far as the common law jurisdictions are concerned, but it's unfounded as far as the most more advanced European countries are concerned. But they won't retry a man. But there's always an exception under the law of France and those other countries in treason or other national security cases because there the foreign country would have a different policy. But everybody is united, all countries, all civilized countries and certainly the states and the nation are united in one common policy against bank robbery. But the mere fact of federal jurisdiction alone cannot create a separate policy. That seemed to be sufficiently clear that couldn't be done, but we can go back to the fact that the states are free to enforce federal, protect federal rights in the early part of the history of our country. That was the standard way for the first half century, I believe. The states were largely relied upon to protect federal rights. It's counterfeiting. And a state could pass a statute making it a crime to rob a bank that's a member of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, for example. I would say that the state having created such a crime and the federal government having also created such a crime makes it necessarily a separate policy because the jurisdictions are different, because the federal government always has a separate policy, is obviously without substance. That's obviously a form of verbalistic conceptualism. Was there an early case, Mr. Fisher, involving this purchase as between federal prostitution for counterfeiting and state prostitution for the same act on the score of fraud? Yes, and they held there were different policies. Sometimes they stated there were different policies because the state policy was directed simply against fraud and the federal policy was to protect the currency. And that may very well be. I do not quarrel with that. You don't quarrel with that? I don't quarrel with any decision that is founded in reason where there is a different policy. But I do quarrel with saying because there are two statutes or two jurisdictions, ipso facto, they are different. That would deprive the Constitution of substance and reduce the double jeopardy provision to a form of words. Well, it wouldn't. It wouldn't, depending on what the limitation against double jeopardy. It binds two different countries. Yes, yes. So you have to clear that level. Yes, Your Honor. A mere identity of a friend doesn't take care of the fact that you've got two different lawmaking bodies. That's as far as I've gone so far. Here's perhaps a good place to mention that a collusive trial never bars a second trial. That is under established common law principles. And the rationale, of course, is that if it was collusive, why, the man was never in jeopardy. Now I'll come to the critical issue of prosecutions by different jurisdictions, where the court finds the offenses would otherwise be the same. In the first place, the defense of formal acquittal is for the protection of the accused. And his need of the protection is identically the same, whether the successive prosecutions are by the same or separate sovereign deeds. The injustice to him is the same. From his standpoint, it is the same. And it is my contention that both on reason and on authority, the two situations should be treated in the same way. The English common law authorities are clearly and sadly on our side. As early as 1678, it was settled in the leading case of Rex against Hutchinson, in our brief, page 40, that a man acquitted in Portugal could not be tried again in England. And there are other cases just as strong. Our brief cites them, and also American colonial materials. Now, there are quite a number of state and lower federal court cases against us. But they do not seem at all persuasive, and neither are certain dicta of this court. And as for the dicta of this court, there are expressions of this court also on our side. And in our brief, we analyze those and fully discuss them. We discussed the liquor prohibition case of United States against Lanza, decided in 1922, which is a week and distinguishable case. It is exclusively argued as a construction of the Volstead Act, and the court, in dealing with the constitutional question, considered only the effect of the 18th Amendment clause which gives the states concurrent jurisdiction, concurrent power to enforce. And this concurrent power to enforce didn't occur. That phrase occurs nowhere else in the Constitution, and it's now out of the Constitution. Furthermore, in Lanza, there had been a prior conviction. It wasn't an acquittal. And the case has been severely criticized by Professor Grant in his article that accompanies our brief by Professor Wexler. The American Law Institute is against it. Now, in this Lanza case, furthermore, the vital common law authorities were not mentioned in the briefs. I've read them. The case has other weaknesses that I go into in the brief. For one thing, the first trial doesn't seem to have been a jury trial, which has an application that I'll come to in a moment. It's clear that the issue of whether the one jurisdiction can retry a man acquitted by the other is still an open question for this court. Now, once Lanza's eliminated, the only remaining argument for double trials is that the federal-state relationship requires it. The argument implies that expediency and the practicalities of American federalism require us to do something that is otherwise constitutionally treated as an injustice and something which England and France, for example, will not do as between foreign countries. Now, I propose to show that not only does American federalism not require such a shameful result, but that in practice and policy, federal-state relations would be improved. If we don't have it, it'd actually be harmed by the extension of any such rule. The heart of the argument, of course, is that unless the state is allowed to relitigate federal criminal judgments, the federal government would equally be prevented from relitigating state judgments. And that would be a limitation on the federal judicial power. Now, I think the rule ought to work both ways, state and federal and federal and state. But we do not agree that the federal government can or should try a man over again who's been acquitted by the state. For one thing, the Seventh Amendment prevents it, at least if the man was tried by a jury. That's why I alluded to the fact that I can't find any evidence that in Lanza the man was tried by the state of Washington jury. But there was a jury in the case of Bob. A petitioner was acquitted by a jury. In this connection, I refer to the second clause of the Seventh Amendment, which is a relatively unfamiliar part of it. Unfamiliar, at least, as I judge, because there are cases on it. Here's what it says. I'll read it. No fact tried by a jury should be otherwise reexamined in any court of the United States than according to the rules of the common law. So the man can't be retried anyway by the federal government if he had a jury trial. So we don't need to perpetuate this injustice or extend it in order to allow the federal government to retry a man because the Seventh Amendment prevents him from being retried anyway. So don't you think the beginning of Article 7 governs the whole of it in suits of common law? Is the criminal trial a suit of common law in that sense? The Seventh Amendment is generally entitled in the manuals civil trials. That's not the manual entitled it, but just its own word. I wouldn't curb it or confide it by the manual label, but in suits of common law. Well, this court has found, your honor, that the second clause is a substantial and independent clause. But let's suppose that it only applies to civil trials. And I'll now accept that for the purposes of further discussion. I don't agree with it, but in view of what this court has said it needs to be independent. I don't know. You don't agree and I don't know. Well, I don't agree with it, but I'll accept it and say it only applies to civil trials. But look where this brings us. It is impossible to believe that when the Bill of Rights was adopted, the jury verdicts in criminal cases were intended to be given less protection than in civil cases. And certainly at that time, the general public sentiment was at least as much concerned with criminal matters as with civil. Therefore, if the second clause of the Seventh Amendment fails to include criminal trials, it could hardly be because our ancestors intended that state criminal jury verdicts should be subject to re-examination in federal courts. I don't think your historical starting point is correct, however terrible it may seem. There are all sorts of advantages, or rather handicaps, that a defendant had in a criminal case that a defendant in a civil suit did not have. Well, there was a... He couldn't be a witness. He couldn't take the stand, the defendant. He couldn't have a lawyer, etc., etc. In the original Constitution also, I agree, Your Honor, that there was a lot of effort to protect property rights and vested rights. But when they came around to adopting the Bill of Rights, the shoe was on the other foot. And at that time, it would not have been at all popular to have suggested that criminal verdicts could be re-examined. But even... But take on reason. Holmes said, for unanimous court in the Oppenheimer case, it cannot be that the safeguards of the person are less than the safeguards that protect from a liability in debt. And stole against Gottlieb in 305, the United States has the same effect. If the Second Clause of the Seventh Amendment is by any possibility applicable only to civil tribes, it must have been because everybody assumed that the re-examination of state criminal verdicts was forbidden elsewhere in the Constitution. And there was a plain clause in there for which that construction could readily be given, namely, the double jeopardy provision of the Fifth Amendment. It seems to me there's an inescapable inference from the Second Clause of the Seventh Amendment that a federal retrial after a state acquittal is unconstitutional. We have some historical materials that we cite in our brief that support this to some extent. So even if this Court is not convinced by this argument based on the Seventh Amendment, I submit that it is unsound federalism to call another jury of Illinois citizens to try a man over again who has been acquitted by one jury of Illinois citizens. That would be that in order to prevent the exceptional case of an individual going free after one inadequate trial, as the judge thought it was inadequate in this case, it would make a rule that everybody is subject to two real trials. And that is not the way to promote respect for our principles and our courts. And there are other and better ways of protecting federal jurisdiction. Congress can always take over the field to a greater or less extent. There is always federal preemption. The only purpose of a federal retrial is to assert federal supremacy. And the normal way to do this, the normal constitutional way to do it, is through the preemption power and the resources of federal preemption are ample and manifold. It wouldn't be necessary for Congress to take over the whole of any field. That's not an attractive remedy. Concurrent jurisdiction is a great part of our constitutional system. But there could easily be partial preemption. For example, Congress might provide that a state couldn't prosecute for federal bank robbery until, say, 30 days after notifying a United States attorney so that he would have an opportunity to proceed first. That would produce only one trial and would preserve federal supremacy. There's no reason for worrying about losing anything by depriving the federal government of the right to try a man, an acquitted man over again. In our brief, we cite materials that show that double prosecutions are not favored by either the states or the nation. The American Law Institute is against them, and most people don't think they can take place in the state. When the statute against interstate transportation of automobiles, the Dyer Act, was passed, and that was a few years before Lanza, the original draft contained a section prohibiting double prosecutions. But Mr. Dyer explained to Congress that where a man has been tried upon the merits in a criminal matter, and the case has been disposed of, why it is a bar anyway to further prosecution, and they left it out.
